A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same risky-choice study. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching relocated results.

before.justification: V1 reports original LLM choice experiments, a 360-participant human study, behavioral correlations, and fitted behavioral models.

after.justification: V2 retains these empirical results and reports additional behavioral-model fits and robustness checks.

M1.justification: The primary behavioral model changes from standard prospect theory with loss aversion lambda and shared decisiveness beta to a symmetric value function with separately bounded beta_gain and beta_loss. This changes the fitted analysis throughout Section 6 and Appendix C.4. The standard specification remains as an alternative in Appendix C.7.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same three base prospect pairs, gain/loss frames, explicit descriptions, 20- and 100-outcome histories, and U.S. human population. The added prompt-wording checks retain the same risky-choice task and data coverage.

E2.justification: V2 Figure 5 adds Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct to the open-model description–history comparison, although Appendix B.1 does not add it to the model inventory. The restricted prospect-theory and regret-model comparisons are retained, with their original numerical tables preserved.

E3.justification: Appendix B.3 adds a controlled evaluation of three introductory prompt phrasings using four reasoning and four conversational models. This introduces an additional testing protocol; the existing prospect construction, temperature, token limit, and evaluation metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 adds a substantive comparison of dual-beta and standard parameterizations, showing that the interpretation of human behavior depends on model specification. It also adds prompt-wording robustness, a reported 10-versus-50-query check, and bootstrap assessment of clustering stability. Existing history-length, training-stage, and restricted-model analyses are retained or extended.

E5.justification: V1 already reports ten query repetitions and 1,000-replicate parametric-bootstrap confidence intervals. V2 adds a separate 1,000-resample bootstrap of behavioral metrics with significance reporting and describes a 50-query check. Appendix B.2.3 also changes the bootstrap binomial trial count from 10 to 20 without explaining its relationship to the ten repetitions still specified in Section 2.4.

E6.justification: V2 adds dual-beta fits and confidence intervals; explicit human choices now yield sigma=0.87 and gamma=0.79 under that specification, versus 0.04 and 0.13 in the retained standard fit. Figure 5 also revises existing implicit correlations, including Olmo-3-32B-Think's human correlation from approximately 0.36 to 0.15. V1 Tables 1–4 survive as v2 Tables 15–18, but the original standard-model checkpoint fits and confidence intervals are replaced.

T1.justification: Appendix B.2.1 adds the domain-dependent decisiveness definition, the beta_loss/beta_gain loss-aversion proxy, and an argument that pure-loss choices identify the product beta times lambda. These are limited mathematical extensions to the existing prospect-theory framework; the standard and regret formulations are retained.

C1.justification: The central clustering, description–history gap, explanation effects, and mathematical-training claims remain. V2 strengthens contribution positioning in Section 8 by claiming the first systematic behavioral taxonomy of LLMs and one of the first direct tests of competing explanations for behavioral variation.

C2.justification: Section 6.1 replaces the primary interpretation of humans as strongly risk-averse and probability-distorting with similar curvature and weighting parameters to LLMs but asymmetric gain/loss decisiveness. It explicitly attributes the specification-dependent interpretation to lambda–beta confounding. Section 4 also adds an argument against context-window capacity explaining the description–history gap.

D1.justification: Appendix B.2.3 supplies dual-beta initialization vectors and sampling ranges and specifies previously unstated random-initialization ranges for full standard prospect theory. Appendix B.2.1 replaces v1's inconsistent maximum-likelihood/35-lottery description with MSE fitting, aligning it with the procedure already documented in B.2.3.

R1.justification: V2 adds Binz and Schulz (2023), Coda-Forno et al. (2024), and Hayes et al. (2024), and removes Chakravarty and Roy (2009). It also positions the dual-beta specification as a special case of Peterson et al.'s generalized power value model. The broader related-work discussion remains largely intact.

P1.justification: V2 selectively rewrites the study-design explanation and behavioral-model discussion, clarifies description–history terminology, and adds acknowledgments. Appendix C is reorganized to separate dual-beta confidence intervals, alternative models, and retained standard-model results, while the main section sequence remains unchanged.

P2.justification: Figures 1–6 and 13 are redrawn with revised typography, legends, axes, colors, and spacing. Appendix Figures 7–12 are substantially enlarged and relocated while preserving their image content. Fit tables are reorganized around dual-beta parameters and relocated standard results, producing substantial visual restructuring.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful model-sensitivity and robustness analyses and makes the dependence of behavioral interpretations on model specification explicit. However, the revised bootstrap trial count is unexplained, and new estimates and confidence intervals show unresolved discrepancies: GPT-5.1's sigma is 0.87 in Table 1 but its interval is [1.28, 1.35] in Table 7. Together with unexplained Figure 5 result changes, these uncertainties prevent a reliable net-quality judgment.
